findings.title: limitFunction drops all caller arguments
findings.cause: The returned wrapper is `() => limit(() => function_())`, so it never captures or forwards the arguments supplied to the limited function.
findings.impact: Any consumer using `limitFunction(fn, options)` with an argument-taking function receives `undefined` arguments at runtime, breaking the public type signature and documented recipe for per-call inputs such as URLs.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-124 returns a zero-argument wrapper. index.d.ts:133-136 declares the result as `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`. recipes.md:161-163 calls `limitedFetchUrl(url)`. An inline runtime probe returned `{ "limitFunctionArgResult": "missing" }` for `await limitFunction(async value => value ?? 'missing', {concurrency: 1})('sentinel')`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run a probe equivalent to: `const limited = limitFunction(async value => value ?? 'missing', {concurrency: 1}); console.log(await limited('sentinel'));` Expected `sentinel`; current implementation prints `missing`.

findings.title: limit.map omits the index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call uses `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`, so Sets, array iterators, and other iterables receive `undefined` instead of their Array.from index.
findings.impact: This violates the documented `limit.map(iterable, mapperFunction)` contract for iterable inputs and silently breaks mappers that depend on stable item positions.
findings.evidence: index.js:106-114 computes `iterableIsArray` and passes `undefined` for non-arrays. readme.md:78-84 and index.d.ts:30-43 state that the mapper receives the item value and index and is equivalent to `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index))`. Runtime probe output for `new Set(['a', 'b'])` was `["a:undefined", "b:undefined"]`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run: `const limit = pLimit(2); console.log(await limit.map(new Set(['a', 'b']), (value, index) => `${value}:${index}`));` Expected `["a:0", "b:1"]`; current implementation returns `["a:undefined", "b:undefined"]`.

findings.title: Options object changes rejectOnClear default from false to true
findings.cause: When `concurrency` is an options object, destructuring defaults `rejectOnClear` to `true` instead of the documented `false`.
findings.impact: `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` unexpectedly rejects pending promises on `clearQueue()`. Consumers that adopted the options-object form without opting into rejection can see new `AbortError` rejections and failing `Promise.all` flows.
findings.evidence: index.js:6-8 destructures `rejectOnClear = true`. readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 document `rejectOnClear` as optional with default `false`. A runtime probe using `pLimit({concurrency: 1})`, one running task, one pending task, then `clearQueue()` observed `defaultClearQueueResult: "rejected:AbortError"`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run: `const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); const running = limit(() => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 25))); const pending = limit(() => 'never'); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); console.log(await Promise.race([pending.then(() => 'fulfilled', error => `rejected:${error.name}`), new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('pending'), 10))]));` Expected `pending` under the documented default; current result is `rejected:AbortError`.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The validation condition is `rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean'`, so falsy non-booleans such as `0`, empty string, or `null` are accepted.
findings.impact: Invalid options silently change behavior instead of failing fast, contrary to the boolean-only API contract and the existing type-level negative test intent.
findings.evidence: index.js:12-14 only throws for truthy non-booleans. readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 define `rejectOnClear` as boolean. index.test-d.ts:29 expects an error for a non-boolean string, but does not cover falsy non-booleans. Runtime probe observed `0:accepted` and `"":accepted` while `1` and `"nope"` threw TypeError.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run: `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0})` or `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: ''})`. Expected TypeError for non-boolean option values; current implementation accepts both.

findings.title: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY concurrency is rejected
findings.cause: The concurrency validator now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency) && concurrency > 0`, removing the prior explicit allowance for `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY`.
findings.impact: Users relying on `Infinity` as an unlimited-concurrency mode now get a TypeError even though the previous implementation accepted it as a positive concurrency value.
findings.evidence: index.js:127-130 rejects non-integers. `git show HEAD:index.js` shows the previous validator allowed `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`. `git diff -- index.js` confirms this allowance was removed. The runtime probe reported `infinity: "threw:TypeError"` for `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run: `pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY)`. Previous implementation accepted it; current implementation throws `TypeError: Expected concurrency to be a number from 1 and up`.
